Hendersonb, Ji-Guang Zhanga,b,⁎ a The Joint Center for Energy Storage Research (JCESR), Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA 99354, USA b Energy & Environment Directorate, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA 99354, USA c The Joint Center for Energy Storage Research (JCESR), Argonne National Laboratory, Argonne, IL 60439, USA d Materials Science Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Argonne, IL 60439, USA e Physical & Computer Sciences Directorate, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA 99354, USA A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Li-S battery Lithium nitrate Coulombic efficiency Cycling stability Lithium metal A B S T R A C T The lithium-sulfur (Li-S) battery is a very promising candidate for the next generation of energy storage systems required for electrical vehicles and grid energy storage applications due to its very high theoretical specific energy (2500 W h kg−1).
However, low Coulombic efficiency (CE) during repeated Li metal plating/stripping has severely limited the practical application of rechargeable Li-S batteries.

In this work, a new electrolyte system based on a high concentration of LiNO3 in diglyme (G2) solvent is developed which enables an exceptionally high CE for Li metal plating/stripping and thus high stability of the Li anode in the sulfur-containing electrolyte.
The tailoring of electrolyte properties for the Li anode has proven to be a highly successful strategy for improving the capacity retention and cycle life of Li-S batteries.
This electrolyte provides a CE of greater than 99% for over 200 cycles of Li plating/stripping.

In contrast, the Li anode cycles for less than 35 cycles (with a high CE) in the state-of-the-art 1 M LiTFSI + 0.3 M LiNO3 in 1,3-dioxolane:1,2-dimethoxyethane (DOL:DME) electrolyte under the same conditions.
The stable Li anode enabled by the new electrolyte may accelerate the applications of high energy density Li-S batteries in both electrical vehicles and large-scale grid energy storage markets. 1.

Introduction Li-S batteries have been studied extensively during the last few decades, yet progress has been slow on critical issues such as high selfdischarge rate, the polysulfide shuttle mechanism leading to a low Coulombic efficiency (CE), and low cycle life [1–3].

More than 80% of recent studies have focused on one electrolyte: lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) in a binary mixture of 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) with LiNO3 as an additive [1–8].

The binary mixture of DOL:DME was originally developed by Mikhaylik and Akridge (Sion Power Corporation) for its excellent rate capability at low temperature, while LiTFSI is used because it is one of the most stable salts in the presence of polysulfides and their corresponding radical reactions [9,10].

Since the breakthrough discovery by Mikhaylik in 2008 of the reduced impact of the polysulfide shuttle achieved by the addition of LiNO3 [11], this salt has become a universal additive in nearly every reported Li-S battery study [7,12].

The effect of LiNO3 on the passivation of Li metal surfaces has been thoroughly studied [5,13–16], with the surface layer often described as one or more LixNOy species, as first suggested by Aurbach et al.[17] This surface (passivation) layer is commonly referred to as a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) [18].
This layer is formed by reactions between the Li metal and electrolyte and its composition is highly dependent on the electrolyte formulation.
An ideal SEI should limit or prevent further reactions of the electrolyte, as well as Li metal dendrite growth at the Li surface (during Li metal plating).
Another desired property is that the SEI only conducts Li+ ions, while preventing electrons from reducing the electrolyte (i.e., it serves as an electronic insulator).

This requires that it have a uniform morphology and composition to ensure a homogeneous current distribution and it should be elastic and flexible to maintain its shape during volume changes which occur upon plating and stripping of the Li metal [18,19].

However, SEIs formed in most http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.nanoen.2017.09.015 Received 1 July 2017; Received in revised form 6 September 2017; Accepted 6 September 2017 ⁎ Corresponding author at: The Joint Center for Energy Storage Research (JCESR), Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA 99354, USA.

liquid electrolytes tend to crack during repeated electrochemical cycling.
The freshly exposed Li in the cracked regions leads to formation of more SEI by decomposition of the electrolyte, as well as promote dendrite formation.

Various approaches, such as the addition of additives or ex-situ formation of an artificial layer, have been explored during the last decade in attempts to achieve the formation of high quality SEIs [20–23].

Although it is well established that LiNO3 is critical in preventing the polysulfide shuttle, to the best of our knowledge, a careful study on the effect of this salt's concentration on the performance of Li metal anodes and Li-S batteries and its fate after long-term cycling has yet to be reported.
In this work, we show that LiNO3 is very effective in forming an SEI layer on Li metal which is distinguished by the inclusion of Li2O.
Electrolytes without LiNO3 do not contain Li2O as an SEI component.

The greatly enhanced CE and prolonged cycle life of electrolytes with a high concentration of LiNO3 strongly suggest that Li2O is a beneficial SEI component, acting to prevent excessive decomposition of the electrolyte.
During repeated stripping and plating of Li metal, LiNO3 is consumed in a self-limiting manner as it passivates freshly exposed Li surfaces.
The morphology of deposited Li metal in the high concentration LiNO3 electrolyte is found to be “nodule-like” with particle sizes in the range of ~5–20 μm.
The SEI replicates the underlying “nodule” particle (3D) surface structure and the SEI growth during each cycle results in a layer of porous residual SEI which continuously builds-up.
The use of electrolytes containing high concentrations of LiNO3 therefore is a promising means to significantly extend the cycle life of Li-S batteries. 2.
Materials and methods 2.1.
Electrochemical measurements CR2032 coin-type cells were used for all tests, with the exception of the in-situ FTIR experiments and NMR experiments.
The electrolytes were prepared by dissolving the desired amount of salt(s) into the solvent(s) in an MBraun LABmaster glove box with an Ar atmosphere (< 1 ppm O2 and < 1 ppm H2O).
Battery-grade DME and DOL were obtained from BASF Corporation.
The diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (diglyme, G2) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (> 99.5%) and was dried over 4 Å molecular sieves prior to use.
LiTFSI was obtained from BASF and LiNO3 was obtained from Alfa-Aesar (98%).
These salts were dried for four days under vacuum at 120 °C before use.

The Cu||Li coin cells were assembled using Li foil (250 μm thick, MTI Corporation) as the counter/reference electrode, two layers of Celgard 2045 separator with 75 μL of electrolyte added, and Cu foil (All Foils) as the substrate for Li metal plating.
The active surface area of the Cu foil disks was 2.11 cm2.
For galvanostatic cycling, a capacity cut-offwas used for plating and a voltage cut-offof 1.0 V (vs.
Li/Li+) was applied for stripping.
The Li-S cell was assembled using a cathode prepared from multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs, Cheap Tubes Inc.) and PTFE (60 wt% aqueous dispersion, Sigma-Aldrich) in a weight ratio of 80:20.
The cathode containing the MWCNTs and PTFE was rolled into a freestanding film and then punched into a disk (1.6 cm2).
The total mass of the MWCNT/PTFE electrode was 5.8 mg/cm2.

The electrolyte used contained the sulfur source in the form of dissolved polysulfides: 50 μL of [0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2 + Li2S8 (2 M based on S) which is equivalent to 3.2 mg of elemental sulfur.
This mass of sulfur is what the reported values of specific capacity are based offof.
The theoretical nominal capacity of the cell is 5.36 mAh (1675 mAh/gsulfur).
The anode was a Li chip (400 μm thick, MTI Corporation) and two layers of Celgard 2045 separator were used.
The Li-S cell was cycled at 0.4 mA/ cm2 (200 mA/g) between 1.9 and 2.7 V which is approximately C/7 rate.
A Lanhe battery testing station and a temperature control chamber set to 30 °C were used to control all galvanostatic cycling protocols.
The cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry studies were controlled with a Model 600E potentiostat from CH Instruments. 2.2.

Spectroelectrochemistry A Thermo Nicolet iS50R FTIR spectrometer with a liquid Ar cooled MCT high D* detector and a spectral resolution of 0.5 cm−1 was used for the FTIR spectroelectrochemical measurements.
The spectrometer was housed in an Ar-filled glovebox to ensure minimal interference from oxygen and moisture.
The measurements were conducted using a home-built ATR electrochemical window cell (Fig.
S13) similar to those used by others [24], and a VeeMAX III ATR accessory with a 45° silicon prism (Pike Technologies, Madison, WI).
The cell was sealed onto the ATR accessory and prism using a Kalrez® O-Ring.
The angle of incidence was set to 50°.
The working electrode was prepared directly on the prism surface as follows: First, the native oxide was removed using an HF etch.
The prism was then immediately transferred into vacuum to minimize exposure to air and oxide formation, and 100 nm of Cu was sputtered onto the prism surface.
The Cu-coated prism was transferred from the vacuum chamber to the glovebox for FTIR measurements without exposing it to air.

Ohmic contact to the working electrode was made using a Pt pin to contact the Cu surface via a separate borehole external to the solution compartment to ensure that electrochemical reactions occur on the Cu surface and not the Pt pin.
An Autolab potentiostat (Metrohm) was used to make the electrochemical measurements.
The potential of the cell was controlled using a leakless Ag/AgCl reference electrode (Warner Instruments).
A Pt coil housed in a fritted glass chamber (BASi, Inc) served as the counter electrode. 200 interferrograms were acquired and averaged to form one absorbance spectrum every 2.25 min.
The spectra were then subtractively normalized to the first spectrum in the series to create a series of difference spectra. 2.3.

Characterization The morphologies of the Li plated on the Cu and Li substrates and the residues on the Cu substrates after stripping were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) on an FEI Quanta 650 ESEM at 5.0 kV and 0.17 nA.
XPS measurements were performed using a Specs PHOIBOS 150 hemispherical energy analyzer using a monochromated Al Kα X-ray source.
The load-lock of the analytical UHV system is connected directly to a glovebox, enabling opening of coin cells and loading of samples without any exposure to ambient atmosphere.

Samples were rinsed overnight in purified G2 (H2O content < 1 ppm) after removal from the coin cell in order to remove residual salt, followed by an additional ~ 1 h rinse in fresh G2 before loading into the UHV system.

Although it is possible that the rinsing process does modify the surface speciation, the relative differences observed between samples are still meaningful as all samples were prepared using the same protocol.
Survey spectra were measured using a pass energy of 40 eV at a resolution of 0.2 eV/step and a total integration time of 0.4 s/point.
Core level spectra were measured using a pass energy of 20 eV at a resolution of 0.05 eV/step and a total integration time of 0.5 s/point.
Deconvolution was performed using CasaXPS software with a Shirleytype background and 70-30 Gaussian-Lorentzian peak shapes.
Peaks were charge referenced using the position of aliphatic carbon in the C1s peak at 284.8 eV.

The ionic conductivity values of the electrolytes were determined using a multichannel conductivity meter with an integrated frequency response analyzer (MCS-10, Biologic Science Instruments) at 25 °C.

The viscosities of the electrolytes were measured using a Brookfield DV-II+ Pro viscometer at room temperature (23 ± 2 °C). 1H, 19F, 7Li and 13C solid state nuclear magnetic resonance (SS- NMR) spectroscopy were performed on a 600 MHz (1H resonance frequency) solid state NMR spectrometer (Bruker, Germany) with 2.5 mm magic-angle-spinning (MAS) probe at a spinning rate of 35 kHz and at ambient temperature (~ 26 °C).
All NMR spectra obtained by Fourier transform of free induction decay after a single pulse excitation with π/ 2° pulse of 4 μs except for the 7Li NMR which instead utilized a π/20° B.D.
The samples were transferred to the rotors in a glove box and moved to the magnet in a double-sealed container to avoid air contamination.
During the MAS experiments, dry nitrogen gas was used to spin the rotor.

To gather enough material for the SS-NMR analysis, Li||Cu pouch cells were assembled at the Advanced Battery Facility (ABF) at the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory using pouch cell assembly equipment from Media Tech.
Cu foil (10 μm thick) at a standard size of 55.5 × 37.5 mm and 80 μm Li foil laminated on the Cu foil were stacked between polypropylene separators for single layer pouch cells.
The electrolyte (1.5 g) was injected into the pouch cell and then sealed under −90 kPa vacuum.
In a temperature control chamber at 25 °C, the pouch cells were cycled at 0.4 mA/cm2 to a deposition capacity of 1 mAh/cm2 and a stripping cut-offof 1 V for 100 cycles by an Arbin battery tester. 3.
Results and discussion 3.1.

Design principles for LiNO3-containing electrolytes After testing the CE for Li metal plating/stripping with the state-ofthe-art electrolyte (1 M LiTFSI in DOL:DME) with and without LiNO3 (Fig. 1a), we found that a high CE (> 99%) is only achieved when the LiNO3 additive is used.
In the work of Li et al. more cycles were obtained with 5 wt% LiNO3 than 1 wt%., suggesting that the LiNO3 additive is consumed during repeated Li plating/stripping cycling [25].
In this study, these authors reported that the maximum concentration of LiNO3 in 1 M LiTFSI in DOL:DME is approximately 0.75 M [25].
As shown by Henderson et al.
[26,27] at room temperature, LiNO3 forms a solid crystalline complex when added to pure DME, even for dilute concentrations, and LiNO3 is insoluble in pure DOL.
The binary DOL:DME solvent system is thus required to achieve even the relatively low salt dissolution limit of 0.75 M.

In contrast, LiNO3 is highly soluble in the higher order glyme solvents with the crystalline solvates formed having a low melting point, thus enabling the preparation of solutions with high concentrations of LiNO3 [27].

Although various concentrations of LiNO3 have been examined up to 5 wt% in DOL:DME, the concentration effect of LiNO3 has typically been masked or down-played with respect to the role of dissolved polysulfides on the plating/stripping behavior of Li metal [25,28].
The main issue which has hampered studying the LiNO3 concentration effect in DOL:DME is its limited solubility in this solvent system.

By switching to a different solvent (diethylene glycol dimethyl ether or diglyme (G2)), we were able to solubilize up to 4 M LiNO3, thus allowing an examination of an extended LiNO3 concentration range relative to DOL:DME (< 0.75 M).
The Coulombic efficiency (CE) of Li metal plating and stripping in a series of LiNO3/G2 electrolytes was tested using Cu||Li half cells with Cu serving as the working electrode (Fig. 1b).
A roughly linear increase in the number of cycles attained before a decrease in the CE is observed with increasing concentration of LiNO3 from 1 M to 4 M.
It should be noted, however, that the maximum CE achieved with LiNO3/G2 mixtures is only ~ 96%.
This is notably lower than what is observed in Fig. 1a for the 1 M LiTFSI + 0.3 M LiNO3 in DOL:DME electrolyte and what has been reported for 1 M LiTFSI + x wt% LiNO3 in DOL:DME electrolytes [25,28].
We found that mixtures of LiTFSI and LiNO3 are necessary to increase the CE of the Li Fig. 1.

As displayed in Fig. 1c, both solvent systems (DOL:DME and G2) can achieve a high CE with a low concentration of LiNO3 (0.3 M), although the number of cycles is limited.
The DOL:DME solvent system gives a slightly longer cycle life compared to G2, however, in the present work, we will focus on the effect of LiNO3 salt rather than the solvent system.
The use of LiTFSI as a co-salt is more critical to Li plating/stripping than the solvent selection.

This phenomena can be attributed to the more facile solvation and desolvation of Li+ cations in the presence of the TFSI- anion (e.g., its weaker coordination strength and reduced ionic association as compared to NO3 -) [27].
Mixtures of LiTFSI and LiNO3 were added to G2 in different ratios and the CE was tested in Cu||Li cells.
The electrolyte was optimized for maximum number of cycles at high CE and this optimized composition was found to be 0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3 in G2.
This is a saturated mixture of LiTFSI and LiNO3 in G2 and corresponds to roughly 0.6 mol of LiTFSI and 3.6 mol of LiNO3 per kg of G2 (i.e., 0.6 molal LiTFSI and 3.6 molal LiNO3).
Fig. 1d compares the CE for the most widely used electrolyte for Li-S batteries (1 M LiTFSI + 0.3 M LiNO3 in DOL:DME) to the new electrolyte formula (0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3 in G2).
Although LiNO3 is effective in providing > 99% CE for Li plating/stripping for the state-of-the-art electrolyte, the cycle life for the Li anode at this high CE is limited to less than 35 cycles.
By increasing the concentration of LiNO3 by tenfold in the new electrolyte, Li can be cycled for > 200 cycles at > 99% CE. 3.2.

Characterization of [0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2 To fully realize the benefits of sulfur cathodes over intercalation cathodes currently used in Li-ion cells, high loading (high capacity) cathodes need to be used.
This means that relatively large amounts of Li metal will be stripped and plated, in excess of 15 μm.
In Fig. 2, a Cu||Li cell is cycled with the new electrolyte to a capacity of 6 mAh/cm2 (~ 30 μm Li) at a current density of 0.6 mA/cm2 (C/10).
Even at this high capacity, Li cycles with > 99% CE (Fig. 2a).
The CE only begins to decrease slightly after 50 cycles (Fig. 2b).
The morphology of Li deposited onto and subsequently stripped from the Cu surface is shown in Fig. 3 for the first deposition/stripping cycle.
Here a new electrolyte was prepared as a reference without any LiNO3 (1 0.4 M LiTFSI in G2) to study the effect of LiNO3 on the CE and morphology.

Although the total salt concentration (LiTFSI + LiNO3) plays a role in both the CE and morphology of deposited Li [29], this composition was selected as a reference, since opposite of LiNO3, pure LiTFSI has a limited solubility (< 2 M) in the G2 solvent.
The physical properties of these two electrolytes are shown in Table S1.
Li deposited from the electrolyte which does not contain LiNO3 possess a random particulate and rod-like morphology (Fig. 3) commonly recognized and categorized as dendritic Li.
In contrast, the G2-based electrolyte with a high concentration of LiNO3 shows a smooth, uniform nodule-like morphology (Fig. 3b).
This morphology is almost identical to that of the Li deposited from a 4 M LiFSI/DME electrolyte which resulted in ultrahigh CE values of up to 99.8% [29,30].
Of equal importance is the visualization of the stripped surfaces.
The insets of Fig. 3c, d show optical images of the Cu surfaces after stripping the deposited Li in the two electrolytes to a voltage cut-offof 1 V vs.
A thick silver/grey layer remains on the Cu surface after stripping in the 1 M LiTFSI/G2 electrolyte (Fig. 3c).
This is “dead Li” which cannot be removed due to electrical isolation.
Dead Li is the direct result of a thick, insulating SEI which forms on the deposited Li surface leading to loss of contact with the current collector [31].
In contrast, a very thin, black film remains on the Cu foil after stripping in the [0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2 electrolyte (Fig. 3d).
The SEM image of this residue has the appearance of a sheet which was presumably the thin and dense SEI layer coating the nodular particles of Li metal.
The corresponding CE measurements for the 1 M LiTFSI/G2 and [0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2 electrolytes are displayed in Fig.
Only about 20% of the deposited Li is successfully stripped in the 1 M LiTFSI/G2 during each cycle and the remainder is built up as dead Li.

In contrast, with the nitrate-containing electrolyte, the CE is > 99% after the first few cycles and the small parasitic loss is related to the formation of additional thin, dense SEI layer content during each cycle.
This will be discussed in more detail below.

Solid state nuclear magnetic resonance (SS-NMR) spectroscopy (1H, 19F, 7Li and 13C) was performed on the residual material build-up on the Cu electrodes of the Cu||Li pouch cells to determine the chemical compositions of the residues formed in the two different electrolytes (Figs.
From the 7Li spectra (Fig.

S2), the integrated areas under the metallic Li peaks (~ 264.9 ppm), corresponding to dead or inactive Li remaining on the Cu electrode after cycling, and the nonmetallic Li peaks centered at around 0 ppm were used to calculate the relative quantities of these two types of Li in the SEI residue formed in each electrolyte.
For the 1 M LiTFSI/G2 electrolyte, there was a significant amount of metallic Li remaining in the residue after cycling.
The ratio of the metallic/non-metallic Li estimated by comparison the area under the peaks was 1:0.8 meaning that there was more metallic than non-metallic Li.
For the nitrate-containing electrolyte ([0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2), the metallic/non-metallic Li ratio was only 1:8.

Comparing the two electrolytes, ten times more inactive Li metal builds up after cycling in the electrolyte which does not contain LiNO3.
For additional comparison, the total residue on the electrodes from the two different electrolytes was weighed after cycling prior to the SS-NMR analysis.

The total buildup on the Cu electrode from the 1 M LiTFSI/G2 electrolyte after 100 cycles (deposition capacity = 1 mAh/cm2) was about 29 mg/cm2, while it was roughly 12 mg/cm2 for the nitrate-containing electrolyte.
Therefore, there is more than twice as much residual mass for the electrolyte which does not contain nitrate.
The non-metallic Li species for the SEI (Fig.

S3b) formed in the nitrate-containing electrolyte were revealed to be Li2O (2.8 ppm), LiOH (0.7 ppm) and LiTFSI (−1.2 ppm) and unclassified components centered at −0.7 ~ −0.8 ppm, which possibly are attributable to LiF (−1.0 ppm) and Li2CO3 (~ 0 ppm), while the Li-containing species are mainly composed of LiOH and LiTFSI for the SEI formed in 1 M LiTFSI/ G2 electrolyte [32].
The 1H, 13C, and 19F spectra (Fig.
S3) show peaks from the decomposed species of G2 (13C and 1H) and TFSI- anions (19F).
The large peaks in the 1H (~ 3.2 ppm) [33] and 13C (~ 58 and 70 ppm) [33] spectra are from unwashed G2 and TFSI- anions in the 19F spectra (~ −78 ppm) [34].
The additional 1H peaks at ~ 1 ppm (and 13C peak at ~ 30 ppm) and ~ −1 ppm may arise due to saturated hydrocarbons and LiOH, respectively.
The 19F NMR results show the formation of LiF at 204 ppm.

In practical batteries with an excess of Li metal (i.e., excess anode capacity to extend cycle life), Li metal will be stripped from and redeposited onto the excess Li substrate rather than a Cu substrate, as has been used for the CE measurements.
To more accurately mimic practical cycling conditions and estimate the long-term stability of the electrolytes, Li symmetrical cells were prepared.
S4, Li//Li cells were cycled at 0.5 mA/cm2 to a capacity of 5 mAh/cm2 (C/10 rate).
In this case, the increase in polarization was used as a criterion to determine the practical cycle life of Li metal in the different electrolytes.

Electrolytes based on the DOL:DME solvent system with and without LiNO3 (1 M LiTFSI and 1 M LiTFSI + 0.3 M LiNO3) were compared to the optimized G2 electrolyte with a high concentration of LiNO3 ([0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2).
With no LiNO3, the cell with 1 M LiTFSI/DOL:DME electrolyte had a very limited cycling life.
The polarization began to increase after ~ 200 h and complete cell death occurred (cell voltage > 1 V) after ~ 500 h.
The increase in polarization is attributed to the build-up of an insulating layer on the two Li metal electrode surfaces [35].
When LiNO3 is used as an additive in small quantities (0.3 M), the cycle life is extended substantially from ~ 500 to ~ 1400 h.
Astonishingly, however, the G2-based electrolyte containing a high concentration of LiNO3 (3 M) cycled for over 3000 h and only began to show a very slight increase in the polarization after 2800 h.
This behavior is a substantial improvement relative to the cycle life of the Cu||Li cell at high capacity (Fig. 2) which began to increase in polarization after 50 cycles (i.e., after 1000 h).

This is the difference between exhaustively stripping all of the Li to 1 V and redepositing Li onto a Cu surface for each cycle with the Cu||Li cells, while only a part of Li is stripped and redeposited onto a Li surface in the case of the Li||Li cells.
Although the morphology of Li deposited onto Li (Fig.
S5) looks very similar to that of Li deposited onto Cu (Fig. 3), the Li surface is quickly passivated by an SEI layer which prevents excessive reductive decomposition of the electrolyte.
In contrast, prior to initially depositing Li, the voltage of the Cu electrode decreases from +1 V to a negative voltage when a fresh layer of Li is formed.
During this time and voltage range (+1 to 0 V vs.
Li/Li+), the electrolyte can be electrochemically reduced as shown in Figs.

S6), even trace amounts of parasitic current for reductive side reactions (none ideal CE) can lead to consumption of the electrolyte.
The voltage window for electrolytes containing LiNO3 was determined using linear sweep voltammetry (Fig.
The discharge voltage cut-offin NO3 --containing electrolytes has previously been examined and LiNO3 was found to undergo irreversible reduction at voltages less than 1.8 V [36].
Here, the electroreduction of the nitrate anion (NO3 - + e-→1/2O2- + NO2 -) occurs on carbon at voltages below 1.9 V vs.
Li/Li+, as seen in Fig.
This reaction is clearly dependent on the type of carbon used and its surface composition (i.e., catalytic sensitivity).

Contrary to carbon, this reaction is self-limiting on Li metal surfaces, and Li is passivated by Li2O, which is why the nitrate is not rapidly consumed in the presence of Li metal anodes (as described above).

However, this simple experiment tells us that in Li-S batteries, the discharge cut-offvoltage must be set equal to or higher than 1.9 V or all of the nitrate in the electrolyte will be reduced at the carbon surface.
S7b shows the oxidation sweep for the new electrolyte (0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3 in G2).
The peak at ~3.6 V is attributed to the oxidation of nitrite (NO2 -→NO2 + e-) which is inevitably formed by the contact of LiNO3 with Li metal (LiNO3 + 2Li→Li2O + LiNO2) [37].
However, the evolution of NO2 gas is unlikely to occur unless the voltage of a Li-S battery is allowed to exceed 3.4 V.
Interestingly, the work of Jozwiuk et al. shows that LiNO3 in G2 acts as a stabilizing additive to drastically diminish gas evolution in Li-S cells [13].

A combination of in-situ FTIR and ex-situ XPS measurements were performed, providing complementary information about the organic and inorganic components of the SEI layer, to better understand the surface speciation that develops in this electrolyte system.

FTIR is widely used for characterizing the organic and inorganic components of the SEI formed on Li anodes [38], but a mechanistic interpretation from FTIR data is difficult due to the presence of many overlapping peaks.

In contrast, the use of the spectroelectrochemical technique subtractivelynormalized in-situ FTIR (SNIFTIRS) greatly simplifies the spectral signature and facilitates a mechanistic interpretation by displaying only the vibrational modes which change during the course of the experiment, thus enabling the correlation of these changes to both time and applied potential.
The SNIFTIRS spectra corresponding to the in-situ electrochemical reduction and oxidation of LiTFSI/G2 with LiNO3 are shown in Fig. 4.

The cell potential was swept linearly from 1.2 to −0.2 V (reduction sweep) and then back to 1.2 V (oxidation sweep) at a sweep rate of 0.2 mV/s (Fig. 4a) while recording the spectroelectrochemical response (Fig. 4b).

Although the reduction sweep appears to be free of electrochemical processes in the potential range of 1.2–0.2 V, significant changes are observed in the spectra between 800 and 1200 cm−1 during this portion of the voltammetric scan.
These vibrational bands relate to the LiNO3 and LiTFSI salts [17], and most likely result from changes in adsorption of salt species in the electrochemical doublelayer.
Reductive breakdown of the electrolyte is shown commencing at around 0.2 V, as indicated by a small negative current in the CV.
Concurrently, the intensity of the spectral features between 800 and 1200 cm−1 diminishes slightly (Fig. 4c) due to consumption of the electrolyte near the electrode surface as it decomposes.
As the potential is swept negative of 0.0 V, a large reduction current can be seen, signifying Li electrodeposition.
The corresponding spectra exhibit more pronounced changes relating to reactions of the electrolyte and newly formed Li metal at the anode.
Specifically, broad absorbance bands centered at 898 and 960 cm−1 exhibited a sizeable decrease in intensity (Fig.

This is attributed to the degradation of the TFSI- anion via chemical and electrochemical processes, such as electrochemical reductive breakdown of the electrolyte, electrochemical reduction of Li (which displaces some of the anion from the interface), and chemical reactions of LiTFSI with freshly-formed Li metal resulting in the formation of additional SEI layer content [17].

Several broad absorbance bands centered around 1442, 1300, and 1124 cm−1 appear to increase in intensity, commensurate with the decrease in intensity of the bands at 898 and 960 cm−1 from the degradation of TFSI- (Fig.

These new signals above 1100 cm−1 can be attributed to Li carbonates, N-Ox species, and LixSOy species, resulting from the electrochemical reductive breakdown of the electrolyte components, and subsequent reaction of the breakdown products with metallic Li and LiNO3 [17].

The spectra did not change significantly during the oxidation sweep (Fig. 4d), indicating that the observed spectral changes are due to the irreversible deposition of the organic and inorganic SEI components mentioned above.

The specific assignments of the vibrational modes to particular molecular species and functional groups was not attempted due to the many overlapping spectral signatures of the species present in solution.
The SNIFTIRS spectra for LiTFSI in G2 without LiNO3 displayed only minor differences which can be attributed to reactions of LiNO3 (Figs.
Most notably, the SNIFTIRS spectra recorded in the absence of LiNO3 lacked the appearance of the new vibrational bands at 1442, 1300, and 1124 cm−1.
Broad absorbances between 700 and 1500 cm−1 are more intense for the electrolyte containing LiNO3 [17].
Accordingly, changes to the spectra in this region appear more intense during the course of electrolyte reduction.

The relative intensities of the spectral changes observed in the different electrolytes, combined with the results from cyclic voltammetry, suggest that the presence of LiNO3 is directly related to the enhanced Li electrodeposition and SEI formation, as well as the increased CE.
It also affects the morphology of the Li deposition (nodular vs. dendritic) formed in these two electrolytes.

To investigate how speciation develops after more extensive cycling, ex-situ XPS measurements were performed on Cu||Li coin cells that had been cycled 100 times (0.4 mA/cm2 current density and 1 mAh/cm2 deposition capacity) using both the 1 M LiTFSI/G2 and 0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3/G2 electrolytes (Fig. 5).
XPS data acquired are from the Cu electrodes for consistency with the FTIR results; however, we note that Li electrodes exhibit essentially identical speciation to that of the Cu electrodes (Fig.
S11), which is consistent with SEM observations of similar Li morphology regardless of the plating surface (Fig. 3 and Fig.

The most notable difference between the two electrolytes is the clear presence of Li2O on the surfaces cycled in the LiNO3-containing electrolytes, as shown by the O1s core level spectra (Fig. 5c), which is consistent with the highly oxidizing nature of LiNO3 and previous literature reports [17].
Quantification of the various surface species (Fig. 5b) also shows lower concentrations of both F and S on the electrodes cycled in the LiNO3-containing electrolyte.
Comparisons of the S2p and N1s core level spectra (Fig.
S12) indicate that this is likely the result of less TFSI- decomposition in the presence of LiNO3.
Also observed in the N1s core level spectra is the presence of NO3/NO2, consistent with earlier observations of LixNOy species on Li surfaces exposed to LiNO3-containing electrolytes [15].

While these anionic species are detected by XPS, we believe they play a minor role in the stabilization of Li metal relative to Li2O since these former species are very soluble in the electrolyte [37].

For the same reason(s) that LiTFSI is detected with both electrolytes, it is likely that some LiNO3/LiNO2 (LixNOy) is trapped amongst the various SEI components or that washing the electrodes after cycling did not fully remove all of the salts.
S7b, the soluble LiNO2, produced by the reaction between LiNO3 and Li metal, can be oxidized at the positive electrode [37].
This clearly indicates that LiNO2 lacks the insolubility requirement of a robust SEI component.
For the complex chemistry of Li-O2 batteries, the function of LiNO3/LiNO2/Li2O has been thoroughly studied by others.
It is generally agreed that LiNO2 is a soluble electrolyte component, whereas the insoluble Li2O beneficially protects the Li metal [37,39,40].
Based on the combination of NMR, FTIR, and XPS results here, we propose that Li2O is the key SEI component responsible for the improved performance of LiNO3-containing electrolytes in Li-S batteries.

Performance of a Li-S battery catholyte Similar to the increased solubility of LiNO3 in G2 over DOL:DME, we found that the G2 solvent also highly favors the solvation of Li2Sn polysulfides (where 4 ≤n ≤8).
The presence of a high concentration of NO3 - anions increases the solubility of polysulfides relative to comparable solutions with only TFSI- anions.

The enhanced solubility of polysulfides in [0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2 relative to 1 M LiTFSI/ G2 is thought to be due to the higher ionic association strength of LiNO3 (than for LiTFSI) [27], similar to LiCF3SO3 in the work of Pan et al.
[41] In fact, we were able to dissolve up to ~ 4 M Li2S8 (based on based on S) in the [0.5 M LiTFSI + 3 M LiNO3]/G2 electrolyte.
The combination of high CE Li plating/stripping and a high concentration of dissolved polysulfides allows us to cycle Li-S batteries with the active sulfur originating in solution.

This concept has been tested in the past [41–44], but was found to have limitations of low cycle life and low energy densities, owing to the limited CE of the Li plating/stripping and limited concentration of soluble active S.
With the electrolyte formulation reported here, however, we are able to cycle Li-S cells with carbon electrodes (containing no sulfur initially) with a low capacity fade rate and ~ 100% CE (Fig. 6).

The first cycle is excluded in Fig. 6a because the Li2S8 in the electrolyte was oxidized first to elemental sulfur (S8 2-→S8 + 2 e-) before full capacity (based on the initial S content in the electrolyte) and stable cycling could occur.
The initial capacity (second cycle) of this cell is 1349 mAh/g (2.69 mAh/cm2) and after 100 cycles it is 1215 mAh/g (2.43 mAh/cm2), corresponding to a capacity retention of 90%.
Typically, a drastic fade in capacity is observed over the first few cycles for Li-S batteries using conventional electrolytes.

This is thought to be due to the dissolution of a certain portion of sulfur, in the form of polysulfides, from the cathode into the electrolyte during discharging/charging which is not able to deposit back onto/into the cathode.
The redistribution and loss of sulfur in the cathode can be completely avoided by starting with sulfur in the electrolyte.
During the first discharge/charge cycle of the cell in Fig. 6, the active sulfur is deposited from the electrolyte in the form of solid Li2S/ S.
Using this method, the limiting factor is the capacity of the sulfur (or Li2S) with which the carbon electrodes can maintain a sufficient electrically conductive network.

This is in contrast to traditional methods, starting with a sulfur (or Li2S) loaded cathode, which are typically filled with excess S (or Li2S) which is electrochemically inactive due to a lack of electrical and/or ionic contact (with the current collector and electrolyte, respectively).

This under-utilized sulfur in electrodes prepared by traditional methods is reflected in a lower capacity (than the theoretical capacity (1675 mAh/g S)) on the first cycle and extensive capacity fade during subsequent cycles.
This outstanding performance using a catholyte is only possible with an electrolyte that allows Li metal plating/stripping to occur with exceptionally high CE. 4.
Conclusions The prevalent electrolytes used for Li-S batteries are based on the DOL:DME binary solvent system with LiNO3 as an additive to prevent the polysulfide shuttle mechanism.
The SEI layer formed on the Li anode surface in the presence of LiNO3 is very stable and the main Fig. 4.

This layer not only suppresses the reduction of the electrolyte co-salt, LiTFSI, and the solvent (G2 in the present study), it also clearly inhibits the reduction of soluble polysulfide species by the Li metal anode.

This, in turn, prevents the polysulfide shuttle mechanism and results in nearly a 100% CE for Li-S cells cycled with a catholyte (i.e., S active material dissolved in the electrolyte) and remarkable capacity retention.
Here, we have shown that LiNO3 is consumed during cycling by chemical reactivity with Li metal.
When used as an additive (i.e., in small amounts), as is the case for the state-of-the-art DOL:DME electrolyte, the beneficial effect of LiNO3 in stabilizing the SEI is limited.
The SEI forms (and reforms) during each cycle, which relatively rapidly consumes all of the additive.

Li-S batteries with a high CE after extensive cycling are enabled, however, by an electrolyte which contains a high concentration of LiNO3 in addition to a second supporting salt to increase the ionic conductivity (LiTFSI).

The high concentration of LiNO3 serves two purposes: 1) to passivate the Li metal negative electrode, thus enabling > 99% CE for Li plating/stripping for an extended number of cycles, and 2) to increase the solubility of Li polysulfides (Li2Sn where 4 ≤n ≤8), thereby allowing the discharge/ charge process to occur via the liquid phase (electrolyte) rather than the reversible solid-state conversion of sulfur (S) to Li sulfide (Li2S).
One of the critical challenges with Li metal anodes is the continuous consumption of the electrolyte during cycling.
Ideally, as with graphite anodes, a stable SEI would form during the first few cycles which would inhibit any further breakdown of salt/solvent components.
In this case, the Fig. 5.

However, as we have shown here, the maximum CE is ~99.5% due to the disruption of the support for the SEI (i.e., stripping of Li).
The small losses (inefficiencies) per cycle are a result of the consumption of LiNO3 during each plating/stripping cycle.
This is evidenced by the direct correlation of the practical cycle life of Li metal (i.e., high CE, > 98%) with the concentration of LiNO3 in the electrolyte.

Although LiNO3 forms a very thin and stable SEI, preventing excessive decomposition of the G2 solvent and TFSI- anions, it forms during each deposition, remains after each stripping of the Li, and thus continuously builds up during cycling.

Strategies to enable practical, longterm cycling of Li metal batteries should focus on both the search for alternative electrolyte additives which are not consumed continuously and also on controlling the morphology of Li metal deposits such that the SEI does not need to grow each cycle and thus the exposure of fresh Li surfaces to the electrolyte can be avoided.
